At a fixed subset size, further training can improve performance, lead to a plateau, or reduce performance. Our law captures smaller-subset advantages that the compared baselines cannot represent and improves prediction at higher budgets on Maxar, SATLAS, and Ego4D under nearest-neighbor evaluation. These findings show that both the number of unique images and how often they are repeated matter when allocating a training budget.

title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
authors: Xinyu Chen, Liangjian Wen, Jiang Duan, Dongkai Wang, Yong Dai, Jiayu Bai, Jianzhuang Liu, Zhen Tian, Guoping Qiu, Zhao Kan
abstract: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.

title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
authors: Yitong Li, Jiang Bian, Jingling Wang, Pan Ding, Chengying Gu, Xing Huang, Hana Song, Dong Zhang, Hao Wu, Yupeng Cui, Longfeng Zhou, Chao Wang, Hua Liu, Zheng Yi, Peng Wang, Haiyang Li, Nan Sun, Fan Yang, Tao Yang, Heng Wang, Yin Liu, Yingpeng Chen, Zouqi Chen
abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
authors: An-Sheng Jhang
abstract: We measure LLM probability updates on $\delta$-SNLI premise-hypothesis pairs across the Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) family. Separate calls elicit priors and posteriors; directional movement s signs changes by the annotated direction. We cross stated vs. reported wording with Direct single estimates (D0) vs. Multi-Candidate Weighted elicitation (MCW; five weighted estimates, V0, weighted mean M_W). Frozen formal tests cover 15 configurations (23,400 planned units): 3 primary (Qwen3-8B thinking off, OLMo-2-7B, gpt-6.1-sol via codex; 6,600), 4 CLI-harnessed configurations (gpt-oss-120b, claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-3.8-flash low/high; dnli-agy; 5,600), and 8 un-harnessed REST API configurations (dnli-api; 11,200). We add a 20-configuration, 8-provider dev ladder (3B-550B; 6,000 units) and a 2-model OpenAI 1+1+4 ablation of D0, Direct-CoT (D_CoT), MCW (V0), and Multi-Candidate Unweighted (MCU; V2 / M_U; 1,800 calls). All 15 reject H1 (s = +16.1 to +28.9 points) and H4a (endpoint reduction +0.065 to +0.391); 13 reject H2 (+2.0 to +8.9 points), except gpt-oss-120b (+0.9) and sf:qwen3.5-4b (-0.64). In 14 of 15 formal configurations, readouts obey Top-1 > MCW (M_W) > MCU (M_U). On 120 common pairs, API Qwen3 tracks local Qwen3 (H1 +18.72 vs. +18.90; H4a +0.265 vs. +0.254; H2 +3.78 vs. +1.67; H4b -9.03 vs. -6.70); local H2 rejects on all 240 pairs (+1.97), not this subset. API Gemma 31B (formal H4b -2.85, Top-1 +0.64; spread -13.3% / +7.6%) and Groq gpt-oss-120b (dev -4.15, +0.40; -18.4% / +12.2%) show small MCW costs and stated narrowing/reported widening without CLI harnesses. In OpenAI ablations, D_CoT keeps numeric-token entropy <1 bit; MCU (V2) shows smaller movement loss but halves spread and $\Delta H_2$ vs. MCW (V0). Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about appropriate update magnitude. Code/data: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

title: IECG: Weakly-Supervised Interpretability-Enhancing Foundation Model for Electrocardiogram
authors: Huynh Dang Nguyen, Trong-Thang Pham, Anh-Thuan Do, Phuong-Nhi Dinh, Brijesh Patel, Ngan Le, Van Nguyen
abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac diagnosis, yet most machine learning methods for ECG analysis lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. We present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without requiring manual abnormal region annotations, overcoming a long-standing bottleneck in interpretable ECG learning. Central to IECG is a weakly-supervised attention strategy that explicitly incorporates clinical priors by deriving abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge. These pseudo-labels guide the model's CLS-token attention through a KL-divergence loss, encouraging it to focus on diagnostically relevant waveform regions. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, enabling it to learn rich multimodal representations while producing localized waveform evidence. By explicitly aggregating features from clinically guided attention regions, IECG grounds its diagnostic predictions in interpretable waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IECG achieves state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance, advancing trustworthy foundation models for ECG analysis.

title: Nominate-then-Adjudicate: LLM-Assisted One-Pass and Per-Instance MIP Solver Tuning
authors: Yifan Zhao, Qianyang Zhao, Xinyu Guan, Kai Wei, Yuming Deng
abstract: Parameter configurations control presolving, cut generation and branching strategies in mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers, directly affecting solving efficiency. Effective configurations vary across instances, while searching for them online requires additional solver runs. We propose Nominate-then-Adjudicate: an empirical performance model (EPM) shortlists candidates from a fixed portfolio, and one large language model (LLM) call selects using static features, compressed formulation text and memory distilled from offline solver measurements. Text exposes distinctions omitted by the chosen aggregate features; selection requires no online candidate solves or foundation-model weight updates. Across sixteen synthetic families, adjudication improves on the EPM's top-ranked candidate (top-1), raising mean normalized performance score from 0.377 to 0.426 and the win rate against SCIP's default from 84.9% to 90.2%; all ten sequential batches show positive mean-score gains. On 400 Ecole instances, it outperforms the per-instance baseline ISAC+ in mean runtime-based score, with gains concentrated in facility location. Total solver time falls by 69.6% versus default, excluding LLM latency. Ablations support text and memory; a second LLM improves over top-1.

title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
authors: Seemandhar Jain, Manmohan Chandraker
abstract: Scientific discovery requires more than generating hypotheses: ideas must be grounded in prior work, translated into executable methods, experimentally validated, challenged by counterevidence, and communicated through reproducible findings. Despite recent advances in autonomous research agents, closing this entire loop remains challenging in rapidly evolving computer-vision fields with complex training pipelines and expensive evaluations. We introduce SplatLab, an autonomous scientific discovery system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that integrates literature understanding, hypothesis generation, implementation, experimental refinement, falsification, and manuscript writing into a unified research pipeline. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, SplatLab identifies research opportunities, proposes novel methods, trains and ablates candidates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, and produces manuscripts grounded in verifiable experimental evidence. Unlike prior systems, SplatLab performs discovery over verified baseline implementations using domain-aligned modification scaffolds. A cascade-weighted Elo tournament evolves candidate methods using measured GPU performance and verbal-gradient feedback, while a standing falsifier incorporates adversarial stress testing directly into selection. An integrity audit binds reported claims to logged experiments, and reviewer-driven feedback can initiate further experimentation rather than merely revising text. SplatLab discovers methods achieving PSNR improvements of +0.18 to +3.78 dB over matched baselines, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, a previously unexplored setting for 3DGS. By closing the loop between scientific reasoning, executable experimentation, and evidence-backed communication, SplatLab compresses months of researcher effort into days of mostly autonomous compute.

title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents
authors: Zehao Lin, Erenkai Zhu, Helan Hu, Xixuan Hao, Chunyu Li, Linyun Liu, Kai Chen, Chenxu Du, Feiyu Xiong
abstract: Language agents carry information from past experience into future tasks whose demands may be unknown or change over time. We develop a decision-theoretic account of the capability available in history, retained in storage and realized through use, together with the costs of recovery and revision. Drawing on comparison of statistical experiments, information acquisition and the value of computation, we express these values in units of avoided task loss. Recovery and revision define attainable risk-cost profiles and preservation across uses. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples establish how information timing, access, computation, feedback and demand shape these comparisons; a pointer with zero answer mutual information can reduce the cost of exact recovery. Allocation and recovery criteria identify when gains pay for estimation, selection and evidence access. Complete-split studies on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S and PersonaMem cover 3,075 questions and two readers. They show complementary value from saved state and recovered evidence, task-dependent performance orderings, and the role of reuse in amortizing construction costs. Multi-project workflows connect correction to preservation and validation costs. Together, the theory and studies support decisions about what to retain, which recovery options to preserve, and how to adapt memory as evidence and objectives evolve.

title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
authors: Tristan Liang, Aravind Nagulu
abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.

title: Scoped Semantic Invariance as a Foundation for LLM Reliability
authors: Rosario Uceda-Sosa, Maria Chang, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Moninder Singh
abstract: LLMs often answer semantically equivalent queries inconsistently, even when the underlying facts are known. We formalize consistency as semantic invariance over equivalence classes of queries and show that invariance under arbitrary meaning-preserving transformations is undecidable in general. This motivates scoped semantic invariance, where model behavior is evaluated relative to bounded semantic domains. We operationalize this framework using knowledge graphs (KGs), which act as explicit semantic control structures defining local semantic constraints and grounding contexts. Across the MITRE D3FEND ontology and eight Wikidata- derived domains, we show that inconsistencies are structured rather than random, concentrating in localized hotspot subgraphs organized around recurring TREE, STAR, and CYCLE patterns that remain stable across models and domains. We further show that selective graph grounding improves correctness and cross-model consistency, while indiscriminate grounding introduces regressions. A layered grounding strategy achieves the strongest monotonicity profile, preserving correct knowledge while reducing inconsistency. Finally, we show that hotspot structures discovered from simple consistency probes transfer to more realistic compositional reasoning tasks.

title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
authors: Hadley Black, Arya Mazumdar, Barna Saha, Geelon So
abstract: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $\Theta(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Heged\"{u}s 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $\Theta(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.

title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
authors: Guoqiang Hu, Lichao Zhang, Yizhou Peng, Yuhao Luo, Haifeng Hu, Zhongqian Sun, Wei Yang, Eng Siong Chng
abstract: When a user talks over a full-duplex dialogue model, it must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can improve this discrimination or change how readily it stops. In our GRPO runs the second dominates: no configuration lowers both error rates on more than one model, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better than their bases. We trace this partly to how the reward is estimated. The probability of stopping inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities the policy emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A group of rollouts that all agree gives no gradient, even when all fail; the push on the stop threshold is strongest where the model is unsure, whichever outcome is right; and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Confining the credit to the window removes only that leakage. Window likelihood (WL) samples the words but integrates over the stop decisions, so the probability of the correct outcome is computed exactly and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates by more than their confidence intervals, without talking into silence.

title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis
authors: Yutian Pang, Yifang Tian, Xinyu Zhao, Jueming Hu, John-Paul Clarke, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
authors: Oz Amram
abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love trains", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, perform far worse. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.

title: Are Spiking Neural Networks Harder to Steal? The Role of Stochastic Encoding in Model Extraction
authors: Ayana Moshruba, Maryam Parsa
abstract: Machine learning models deployed on edge devices are vulnerable to model stealing attacks, in which an adversary replicates a model using only its predictions. Existing defenses add mechanisms that are costly on resource-constrained hardware. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer energy-efficient inference at the edge and have been shown to leak less information about their training data than artificial neural networks (ANNs). This work investigates whether SNNs also resist model stealing and identifies the source of any such resistance. We evaluate four model stealing attacks against SNN and ANN models on three image datasets and introduce a metric that accounts for the stochastic outputs of SNNs. SNNs exhibit greater resistance than ANNs: on average, surrogate models extracted from SNNs agree with their targets 38% less often outside the training distribution, and targeted adversarial examples crafted on these surrogates transfer 54% less often. This resistance, however, arises mainly from the randomness of their input encoding rather than from their spiking computation, and an adversary who repeats each query can largely overcome it. SNNs therefore protect against model stealing without additional defense mechanisms, but this protection does not withstand adaptive adversaries.

title: Learning Where to Trust: Reliability-Guided Expert Routing and Velocity Gating for 3D Deformable Registration
authors: Chenyu Guo, Wenjie Dai, Yiqian Chang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yunfan Wei, Shuhan Qi, Tianrui Xu, Dong Liu, Ming Cong
abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.

title: Text Generation in Low-Resource Languages Using Human-Curated Vocabularies
authors: Michael Christlambert Sinanta, Muhammad Dehan Al Kautsar, Amanda Nurul Izzah, Thanh-Nhi Nguyen, Phan Phuong Mai Chau, Zheng Wei Lim, Fajri Koto
abstract: Synthetic text generation offers a promising approach to alleviating data scarcity in low-resource languages. However, its effectiveness is inherently limited for languages that are scarcely represented, or entirely absent, in an LLM's pretraining data. At the same time, many such languages have human-curated vocabularies that provide rich lexical and semantic information, often accompanied by grammatical information such as part-of-speech labels. In this work, we ask whether LLMs can leverage these resources to generate coherent text in extremely low-resource and unseen languages. We introduce a framework that combines human-curated vocabularies with a small number of human-written exemplars that provide syntactic signals, while sampling candidate words according to a Zipfian distribution. Across languages with varying levels of resource availability, we evaluate the generated text using lexical diversity, off-target ratio, and human judgments of fluency. Our results show that reasoning-enabled LLMs can generate fluent text even in extremely low-resource languages, with particularly strong results at the sentence level and promising performance at the paragraph level. Our findings highlight a practical pathway for bootstrapping synthetic data in low-resource languages, expanding the amount of usable text even when existing digital resources are extremely limited. Our source code is available at https://github.com/michaelsinanta/vocab2text.

title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
authors: Marcos Hernanz
abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.

title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
authors: Albert Bou, Javier Valdes-Aleman, Jon M. Laurent, Samuel G. Rodriques, Andrew D. White, Michaela Hinks, Siddharth Narayanan
abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.

title: Diffusion models for the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model
authors: Daniel Schubring
abstract: A score-based diffusion model is trained on the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model, the lattice representation of the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model. Neural networks are trained on three different coarse-grainings of the same training set to implement a multiscale sampling scheme that modestly improves both the accuracy and computational cost of direct sampling on the finest lattice. Stein (or Schwinger-Dyson) diagnostics for the two-point correlation function are introduced to assess the quality of the learned score without relying on reverse diffusion sampling. These diagnostics are also incorporated into an additional training loss. We discuss several technical considerations relevant to implementing diffusion models on $S^2$. These include a consideration of lifting the network input to $S^3$, as in the $CP^1$ representation, and developing a boundary-layer approximation to the short-time spherical heat kernel that extends its usefulness to larger diffusion times.

title: Textual Response-Aware Guidance for Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
authors: Yubo Cui, Xianchao Guan, Zheng Zhang
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features constrains all directions equally, providing broad coverage without semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. We therefore propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.

title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
authors: Jie Liu, Nicola Bastianello, Wenying Xu, Daniel W. C. Ho, Karl H. Johansson
abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.

title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
authors: Guy Lemieux, Michael L. Overton
abstract: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.

title: Low-Margin Branch Points in Deterministic LLM Deliberation
authors: Hajime Shimao, Warut Khern-am-nuai
abstract: Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.

title: Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer for Joint Multipath Parameter Estimation: Applications to mmWave Positioning and Radio SLAM
authors: Yaya Etiabi, Wessam Ajib, Halima Elbiaze
abstract: Future 6G wireless networks are expected to evolve toward AI-native systems that support intelligent, environment-aware services, including positioning and mapping. Current research has already integrated AI into several aspects of communication, particularly wireless channel estimation. However, most learning-based channel estimators focus on communication-oriented objectives rather than explicitly estimating multipath parameters such as delay, angle of arrival (AoA), and angle of departure (AoD). These parameters provide essential geometric information for downstream tasks including positioning and radio simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). In this work, we propose a Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer (SCFT) for joint multipath component (MPC) estimation from noisy complex channel estimates and physical beam-pair descriptors. SCFT combines local spectral convolution, permutation-equivariant beam-set attention, and a query-based Transformer decoder to detect and classify line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight paths and estimate their observed delays, AoAs, and AoDs. Experiments on realistic ray-tracing data show that SCFT reduces the generalized optimal sub-pattern assignment error by 13.1% compared with ResNet, the strongest competing baseline. We further demonstrate this advantage in independent snapshot positioning and radio SLAM, where SCFT reduces position RMSE by 18.5% and 65.0%, respectively, relative to ResNet. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly recovering multipath geometry, as improvements in MPC estimation can translate into substantial gains in downstream tasks.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
authors: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen, Jiaying Li
abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from -17.3 to -6832 as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). Every single tempering factor we tried, estimated from residuals or tuned on validation data, collapsed in some setting; mixtures over a fixed grid of factors never did. In registered tests on three world-model families trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model in which actions mattered, and reached the registered power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's own token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in all 96 units, 24 of 26 games and 6 of 6 tasks. Under exact nulls the statistics made 4 rejections in 22,848 tests.

title: On Stochastic Continuous-Time Linear System Identification for Adaptive Stabilization
authors: Reza Sadeghi Hafshejani, Mohamad Kazem Shirani Faradonbeh
abstract: System identification studies the canonical problem of reliably learning system-dynamics from state and input trajectories. One of its important applications consists of estimating a feedback gain matrix that can stabilize an unknown system. This paper focuses on the analysis of such adaptive stabilization schemes for multivariate linear time-invariant state-space models. The system instability practically renders trajectories short, i.e., the observed data is notably limited. So, it is crucial to tightly consider effects of \emph{all} involved quantities including length and number of trajectories, dimension, controllability Gramian, and signal-to-noise ratio. We put forward a simple, practical, and reliable relationship between the chance that adaptive stabilization (based on system identification) fails to stabilize the system, in terms of all the above-mentioned quantities. Our findings show that despite exponential effects of all other quantities on failure probability, such effects do not hold for signal-to-noise ratio. More specifically, this study shows that the strength of the excitation signal helps stabilization only \emph{logarithmically}; a very important phenomenon that we explain under the term \emph{signal saturation}.

title: MAGAR: Multimodal Agents for GUI-Based 3D Mechanical Assembly and Minimal Rework
authors: Jingxuan Wei, Jiahao Fu, Fuqiang Wang, Xiaoming Wu, Yuwen Liu, Kaiwen Wei, Ming Yang, Junnan Zhu
abstract: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.

title: FORGE: Fault-Oriented Rework Code Generation for Executable Interlocking Assembly
authors: Fuqiang Wang, Jiahao Fu, Ren Hefeng, Yining Qian, Chuanting Zhang, Cheng Tan, Yuwen Liu, Jingxuan Wei
abstract: Large language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in structured reasoning and code generation, yet identifying an assembly fault does not guarantee the ability to generate executable rework programs. In interlocking assemblies, a locally plausible repair program may violate blocking dependencies, omit required recovery operations, or terminate in an incorrect configuration. We identify this challenge as fault-conditioned executable rework generation, where models must jointly reason about structural failures and generate programs that restore constrained assembly states. To benchmark this capability, we introduce FORGE-Bench, containing 4,000 tasks across 26 interlocking assemblies with five assemblies held out for evaluating generalization to unseen structures. We further propose FORGE (Fault-Oriented Rework Code Generation for Executable Interlocking Assembly), a structured state-to-program framework that decomposes rework generation into Rework Structuring and Action Grounding. Rework Structuring captures fault-induced recovery dependencies, while Action Grounding maps these dependencies into state-conditioned executable actions. Experiments show that locally reasonable repair code is insufficient for reliable assembly recovery, and that connecting structural recovery reasoning with executable action realization is essential for verified target restoration.

title: FindLink: Learning to Assess Scientific Connections from Source-Grounded Premises
authors: Jingxuan Wei, Song Tan, Xiaohan Liu, Chao Sang, Changwei Wang, Linzhuang Sun, Bihui Yu, Fuqiang Wang, Junnan Zhu
abstract: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions. Source attribution makes individual findings traceable, but does not determine what they jointly support. We introduce GI-TraceBench, a benchmark of 10,282 questions in gastrointestinal oncology that unifies provenance question answering, knowledge discovery, and hypothesis evaluation through shared Paper, Claim, and Evidence Span records. We further propose FindLink, a two-stage framework for provenance-grounded scientific reasoning. Premise Grounding constructs source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status. Structured Reasoning organizes these premises into support plans that represent both supported relations and unresolved conditions, then generates evidence-conditioned answers using deterministic compiler feedback. The compiler verifies structural and source-binding consistency, but does not assess scientific entailment. On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone. A retrained variant without Structured Reasoning achieves slightly higher premise-identifier F1, but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1. These results indicate that scientific reasoning requires not only identifying grounded premises, but also assessing what connections those premises support.

title: AGiR: Mitigating Gift Over-Reliance in Mixed-Motive Games
authors: Woohyeon Byeon, Seongmin Kim, Jiwon Jeon, Woojun Kim, Youngchul Sung
abstract: In this paper, we consider mixed-motive games (MMGs) which model various real-world multi-agent scenarios where self-interested agents must both cooperate and compete. We identify an issue with existing gifting methods, where agents become overly dependent on incoming gifts and fail to learn reward-yielding behaviors, a phenomenon we call gift over-reliance. To address this, we propose a refusal-augmented gifting framework that balances cooperation and competition in MMGs. Our approach introduces an adaptive refusal mechanism that allows agents to selectively reject a portion of received gifts from their policy-update signals, thereby mitigating gift over-reliance and preventing the agents from being exploited by other agents. This mechanism is gifting-method-agnostic, serving as a plug-in for existing schemes while enabling decentralized learning. We demonstrate that across diverse MMG environments and gifting schemes, our mechanism consistently reduces gift over-reliance and prevents lock-in to sacrificing policies, improving $\alpha$-fairness as a result, without necessitating major changes to existing training pipelines.

title: Kierston & KierstonBench: Simulation of Allentown, PA and Evaluation of Language Models in Crime Investigation and Surveillance Tasks
authors: Andrew Semenov, Svyatoslav Dorofeev
abstract: Large language models are candidates for collecting and analyzing records in criminal investigations and mass surveillance. Their capability and accuracy in this work cannot currently be measured. Real deployments lack the ground truth needed to score a model's conclusions, and no benchmark evaluates these capabilities in a simulated environment. We present Kierston, a city-scale simulation engine, and KierstonBench, a benchmark that tests these capabilities against known simulated events. Kierston models approximately 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, generating their daily activities and the telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records that surveillance and investigative systems collect about them. These records derive from a common behavioral timeline and are distributed across sources representing separate providers. Models investigate through a restricted records interface, linking observations across sources without access to the underlying simulation. The benchmark comprises 32 task families covering record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation and assessment of deceptive accounts. In an evaluation of sixteen language models, most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support. A small number of frontier models solved most of the tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient. In some cases these models still fell for common deceptions and assumptions, and none replaced an investigator.

title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
authors: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak
abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection (an interference, a balanced interferometric reading or a camera) and the output is a Born probability: attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^2$, the form of the Born rule, normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections a classical controller squares, divides, rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-13}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference the model reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % test accuracy, level within the spread of three seeds with a softmax transformer of the same size (76.62 +- 0.36 %). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of test pairs, out of the 53 % any single deletion can change, against 32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients and 31 % for the Born Transformer's own attention. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics (simulated), and its attention overlaps to Hadamard tests on qubits; a separate coherent attention layer becomes one post-selected circuit (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps, the device gave the model's answers on the two shortest test pairs, also when the one word that decides one of them was deleted; with calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence on one pair (correlation 0.997) and on the other less closely (0.962).

title: Recasting Visual Language Models as EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Neurodiagnostics
authors: Xin Zhou, Elena Sergeeva, Nan Bi, Wenyu Song, Lijun Yin, Hao Deng
abstract: Historically automated electroencephalography (EEG) systems was done using task-specific supervised models trained on purposely annotated data. A more recent modeling paradigm relies on creating a unified representation, or a 'foundation model', for multiple modality-specific tasks through large-scale domain-specific pretraining on the unannotated EEG signal. The quality of this unified representation directly depends on the availability of the modality-specific datasets. At the same time, generalist Vision Language Models (VLMs) exhibit broad few-shot learning capacities as well as good fine-tuning adaptability to different visual and language tasks. Can VLMs learn how to read and interpret EEG visually, emulating to a degree the way human clinicians inspect the EEG patterns? In this work we make a case that they can: we show that generalist VLMs without large-scale EEG pretraining perform competitively across a collection of clinical neuro-diagnostic tasks, can adapt to different tasks in a few-shot learning setting better than specialist foundation models, and exhibit better performance with model scaling when modality-specific models fail to exhibit.

title: Combining Relevant Expert Knowledge Using Mixtures of Feedback Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
authors: Olaoluwa Adigun, Akash Kumar Panda, Bart Kosko
abstract: A neuro-symbolic system should combine only relevant answers from expert agents or other knowledge sources. Using only relevant experts for a given input query becomes ever more important for accuracy and scalability as the knowledge network grows and connects ever more knowledge sources. We extend the standard definition of relevance from the legal theory of evidence: An answer is relevant if and only if it is both probative and material for the matter at hand given the knowledge available. We apply this relevancy scheme to mixing the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps (FCMs) of real or artificial experts. The expert FCM directed causal graphs mix or combine into a common knowledge network. We compare the equilibrium limit-cycle predictions or answers of the experts to the answers of the mixture FCM and then estimate the probative status of answers by their difference or variation. A new Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge mixture into corresponding posterior-like FCMs that also allow relevancy-based comparisons. The result is a final set of relevancy mixing weights that produces a relevancy-mixed FCM knowledge network for the given query. So different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs. We demonstrate this relevancy approach using generated synthetic FCMs from an actual 13-node expert FCM that models the causes and feedbacks of ischemic-stroke risk.

title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
authors: Junbo Jacob Lian, Kaixuan Chen, Hanzhang Qin, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Chung-Piaw Teo
abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
authors: Kuber Shahi, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours. The largest clinical archives restrict redistribution, while public datasets use different formats and licences. Here, we rebuild the 77 redistributable datasets of the REVE pretraining corpus that reach its 200 Hz input (14,075 hours across 7,272 subjects) and release them as eegdash-corpus-v0, with raw-file access by name through EEGDash and a checksummed Zarr store on Hugging Face, converted with REVE's preprocessing recipe. Every dataset keeps its licence, and any subset of datasets can be selected by name. To test whether this public store pretrains REVE-Base, we train the model twice from scratch with REVE's trainer and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. First, under linear probing, the frozen encoder reaches 0.331 in chance-adjusted balanced accuracy, against 0.333 for the released model (untrained: 0.200), a difference smaller than the spread between our two pretraining seeds. Second, after fine-tuning, it reaches 0.273 against 0.325 published (0.301 in our rerun), and part of this gap comes from the scoring pipeline. A public, training-ready EEG corpus can therefore pretrain the frozen representations of a foundation model and provide a shared base that other groups can audit.

title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
authors: Tianwei Zhang, Ivy Njoki Nyagwencha, Zahraa Dirani, Shalini Joshi, Scott A. Hale
abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Zhifeng Li, Zhiming Wang, Xinze Feng, Yongqi Liu, Shanglin Yang, Yang Zhou, Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen
abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

title: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
authors: Tung-Wei Lin, Gabe Fierro, Han Li, Tianzhen Hong, Pierluigi Nuzzo, Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli
abstract: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.

title: Volatility Heredity in Multivariate Time Series: A Statistically Guided Temporal Convolutional Approach to Variable Ordering
authors: Kaoutar El Azaar, Mohamed Hamlich, Moncef Garouani, Franck Ravat, Asmae Chakir, Mohamed Tabaa
abstract: Volatility heredity concerns the information that past fluctuations in one series may carry about another after accounting for the target's own persistence. QS-TCN compares this dependence in both directions to estimate an order of temporal precedence. For each series, quasi-maximum likelihood estimation yields a persistence coefficient, and the matrix pencil method extracts temporal modes from the autocovariances of squared observations. These estimates define filters in a temporal convolutional network. The network models the target's squared observations from their own past and scores the association between the residuals and the filtered history of a candidate source. Differences between the two directional scores are aggregated into a global order. In an exploratory simulation with 100 systems in each of four volatility regimes, an ensemble of ten models trained with fixed seeds achieved higher mean ordering quality than CCF-AUC, a lead--lag method based on distance correlation, in every regime. Against CCF-AUC applied to squared standardized observations, the mean gains were 8.69 percentage points under positive linear coupling and 7.81 points when nonlinear coupling depended on the target's state. In the other two regimes, paired 95\% bootstrap intervals for the gains included zero. Mean agreement with reference constraints was 71.55\% across nine Finance systems and 54.02\% across 27 simulated functional magnetic resonance imaging systems, compared with 50\% expected under random ordering. In a panel of daily currency and gold returns, the estimated order placed the dollar--franc and dollar--yen exchange rates before gold.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
authors: Nischay Dhankhar, Alisher Amantay, Zhanibek Datbayev, Darkhan Akhmetov, Yash Shah, Nurmukhamed Ubaidullayev, Raman Saparkhan, Dos Baha, Abulhair Saparov
abstract: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
authors: Jingsong Liu, Youssef Wally, Han Li, Weiwei Zhou, Jing Dai, Elisabeth Wetzer, Peter J. Sch\"uffler
abstract: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.

title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
authors: Shuyi Miao, Zheng Li, Xu Xie, Linrui Xu, Fei Shen, Xiaoyu Du, Tat-Seng Chua
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
authors: Zhaorui Tan, Jun Aun Tan, Weixiang Zhong, Xiaoxi Wang, Tan Pan, Xingdong Xue, Li Liu, Jing Zhang, Jing Zhang, Weimiao Yu
abstract: Pathology reporting translates tissue observations across regions and slides into diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions, yet explicit tissue-composition measurements are rarely used to guide H&E-based report generation. We developed PathXAI, which pairs transferable tissue segmentation with a pretrained vision-language model. Because supplying tissue information directly with H&E images gave limited benefit, PathXAI-Report uses segmentation overlays and tissue statistics in separate steps, selects between candidate diagnoses by fixed rules, acquires further images when evidence is insufficient and records every step for review, without updating model weights. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than H&E-based comparators. On the public cohort, it exceeded Qwen+H&E by 4.4 percentage points in cancer family match rate and 5.7 percentage points in finding F1.

title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
authors: Gon\c{c}alo Gomes, Bruno Martins, Chrysoula Zerva
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
authors: Ayush Sawarni, Wenqian Xing, Tijana Zrnic, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis
abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

title: Counting Events, Not Seeing Them: Diagnosing and Repairing the Readout Failure in Video LLMs
authors: Dongwu Qian
abstract: Video LLMs fail conspicuously at counting how many times an object crosses the screen, a failure attributed to missing object permanence. Using construction-grounded synthetic testbeds with validated labels, we show this attribution is incomplete: the count signal is present but unread - linear probes decode per-window presence at 93% while global count decoding collapses to a duration confound. Concurrent work reports the same representation-output dissociation for repetition counting; we show that in exit-and-reappear event counting it is repairable: two readout-directed repairs (episode-localization supervision and a discrete event-symbol side channel) raise same-object counting from 46.7% to 65.0% (oracle 66.7%) on a chance-33% benchmark across 7B-30B systems. Transfer to an independent factory costs nothing, and a measurement audit exposes five data-integrity failures that had obscured the boundary. A real-video audit (REALCOUNT, n=18, blind-audited) shows the boundary persists - best 55.6% at chance 33.3% - and symbol transfer fails zero-shot. A 1-epoch in-domain adaptation bench is negative (six levers at 28-50%), but 3 epochs reverse this for the symbol channel: with oracle timelines the reader reaches 94.4% sequence-disjoint (and 100% strict on the full set), while the deployed 2-epoch head reaches 61.1% in all three seeds (42-44), no better than a shuffled-symbol control (61.1% seed 42, 66.7% seed 43), and one clip above the unadapted reader (55.6%). The residual gap is detector evidence, not reader capacity: the same reader reaches 72.2-88.9% on GT timelines. The failure is repairable with informative timelines, but the deployed head remains the bottleneck; a frozen-feature boundary probe is weak (AUC 0.62 vs. 0.51 permutation) and non-transferring (0.77 within-clip vs. 0.62 across windows).

title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
authors: Isaac Saxton-Knight, Gabriel Saxton-Knight, Diego Oliveira, Tidor-Vlad Pricope, Aston Garratt, Jocelyn D'Arcy
abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

title: Veterans' Mental Health Crisis Severity Annotation: Do LLMs Agree More Than Human Experts?
authors: K M Sajjadul Islam, Pranav Yaramalla, Nadiyah Johnson, Mark Flower, Praveen Madiraju, Zeno Franco
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear.
